questions.passage: The museum added a new wing in ______ main entrance remained unchanged.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: 2019, the building's
2019 the building's
2019; the building's
2019: the building's
questions.explanation: The text contains two independent clauses, so a semicolon is needed when no coordinating conjunction joins them. A comma alone creates a comma splice, a colon misleadingly presents the second clause as an explanation, and no punctuation produces a run-on.

questions.passage: Because the snow had fallen steadily ______ the school district delayed the start of classes by two hours.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: overnight;
overnight
overnight,
overnight:
questions.explanation: The opening dependent clause must be separated from the main clause by a comma. A semicolon or colon cannot follow the dependent clause in this sentence, and omitting punctuation makes the sentence unclear.

questions.passage: The award went to Dr. Elena Ruiz ______ for her work on water filters that remove lead.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: , a chemist at a small laboratory in Tucson,
a chemist at a small laboratory in Tucson,
, a chemist at a small laboratory in Tucson
; a chemist at a small laboratory in Tucson,
questions.explanation: The phrase identifying Dr. Ruiz is a nonessential appositive and must be set off by commas on both sides. Missing either comma or using a semicolon before the phrase violates Standard English punctuation.

questions.passage: Every Saturday, Mateo carried his grandmother's letters from the closet to the kitchen table but never opened them. He arranged the envelopes by date, then by postmark, then by the color of their edges. When his sister offered to read one aloud, he said the kitchen light was too dim and returned the letters to the closet.
questions.q: Which choice best describes what the text suggests about Mateo?
options: He is not yet ready to read the letters, though he wants to keep them close.
He has forgotten what the letters contain and hopes his sister will remind him.
He is annoyed that his sister keeps interrupting his housework.
He believes the letters are unimportant and plans to throw them away.
questions.explanation: Mateo repeatedly handles and organizes the letters but avoids opening them and declines his sister's offer, suggesting reluctance even as he keeps them. The passage does not suggest forgetfulness, a plan to discard them, or annoyance about housework.

questions.passage: After a regional railway began offering refrigerated freight in 1904, dairy farms farther from the city could ship milk that stayed fresh long enough to sell. Within a decade, the number of dairy farms within 20 miles of the city fell, while farms 50 to 80 miles away increased. The city's milk supply did not shrink.
questions.q: Which choice best describes an inference supported by the text?
options: Refrigerated freight allowed dairying to expand into areas farther from the city without reducing the city's milk supply.
Refrigerated freight caused the city's overall milk supply to decline sharply.
Farmers within 20 miles of the city produced more milk than before.
The railway stopped serving farms located within 20 miles of the city.
questions.explanation: The passage says farms farther away increased while the city's milk supply did not shrink, supporting the inference that refrigerated freight allowed dairying to spread outward. The other choices contradict the text or add unsupported details.

questions.passage: A student argues that Ridgeline's expanded weekend bus service helped workers who have evening shifts. The service began in March and runs until midnight on Fridays and Saturdays. To support this argument, the student wants to use a finding about workers in Ridgeline.
questions.q: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the student's argument?
options: After the expanded service began, late-shift workers at a Ridgeline distribution center reported 25% fewer missed shifts caused by transportation problems than they had the previous year.
Ridgeline's bus system costs about $1.2 million per year to operate.
Most Ridgeline residents who work evening shifts own a car.
The expanded service carries more passengers on Saturday afternoons than on weekday mornings.
questions.explanation: The claim is that expanded weekend bus service helped evening-shift workers. Evidence of fewer transportation-related missed shifts among late-shift workers after the service began directly supports that claim; passenger timing, operating cost, and car ownership do not establish the same benefit.

questions.passage: A team of ecologists hypothesized that replacing cool-white LED streetlights with warmer amber lights would reduce the number of migratory birds drawn off course through the town of Cedar Hollow. To test the hypothesis, the team plans to compare bird activity under the two lighting conditions.
questions.q: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the hypothesis?
options: During the same migration season, streets with amber lights recorded substantially fewer birds circling and calling at night than streets with cool-white LEDs did.
Amber lights used less electricity than cool-white LEDs did.
Cool-white LEDs were more common in neighborhoods near the river.
Birdwatchers reported seeing more birds in Cedar Hollow's parks during the day.
questions.explanation: The hypothesis concerns whether amber lights reduce birds being drawn off course at night. A direct comparison showing fewer nighttime circling and calling birds under amber lights supports it; energy use, daytime sightings, and light placement do not test that effect.

questions.passage:
• Program: after-school coding club at Franklin Middle School
• Started with 12 students in September
• By May, 48 students attended weekly
• The club added a girls' robotics team in February
• Survey: 85% of members said they felt more confident solving problems
questions.q: A student has taken the following notes about an after-school coding club. The student wants to write a sentence for a school newsletter that emphasizes the club's growth over the school year. Which choice best accomplishes the student's goal?
options: Franklin Middle School's coding club meets weekly and uses problem-solving activities.
The coding club started in September and added a girls' robotics team in February.
The after-school coding club grew from 12 students in September to 48 weekly attendees by May and added a girls' robotics team in February.
A survey found that 85% of coding club members felt more confident solving problems.
questions.explanation: The correct sentence gives the starting and later attendance numbers and notes the addition of a robotics team, directly emphasizing growth. The other choices either omit the growth numbers or focus on confidence and basic scheduling.

questions.passage:
• The city held its first Riverbend Book Festival in May.
• The festival featured 40 authors and drew 9,000 visitors.
• A downtown café reported a 22% increase in sales during the festival weekend.
• A local bookstore sold 1,100 books, about three times its usual weekend total.
• A survey found that 68% of out-of-town visitors said they planned to return.
questions.q: A student has taken the following notes about a book festival. The student wants to write an introductory sentence for an article arguing that the festival benefited downtown businesses. Which choice best accomplishes the student's goal?
options: The Riverbend Book Festival was held in May and was the city's first book festival.
The Riverbend Book Festival featured 40 authors and attracted 9,000 visitors to the city.

During its first weekend, the Riverbend Book Festival drew 9,000 visitors, while a downtown café reported a 22% increase in sales and a local bookstore sold about three times its usual number of books.
A survey found that 68% of out-of-town visitors to the Riverbend Book Festival planned to return.
questions.explanation: The correct sentence links festival attendance with a café's sales increase and a bookstore's unusually strong sales, directly supporting the claim about downtown businesses. The other choices mention attendance, return plans, or timing without reporting business gains.

questions.passage: Residents such as Elena Ruiz initially worried that the new bike-share program would serve mainly tourists. After a year, however, records showed that most riders were local commuters, a finding that ______ the critics' concerns.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
options: ignored
confirmed
multiplied
eased
questions.explanation: The evidence that most riders were local commuters reduced the critics' worry that the program would serve mainly tourists. "Confirmed" is incorrect because the finding works against the original concern rather than supporting it.

questions.topic: Form, structure and sense (grammar and usage)
questions.passage: Rosa is one of the students who currently ______ at the community garden every Saturday, helping to water vegetables and distribute produce.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: volunteer
volunteered
volunteers
is volunteering
questions.explanation: The relative pronoun "who" refers to the plural noun "students," so the present-tense plural verb "volunteer" is needed. "Volunteers" is tempting because it agrees with "one," but the clause describes the students, not Rosa alone.

questions.passage: The neighborhood association, led by Tasha Moore, expected the new community garden to reduce grocery costs for nearby families. ______, a survey after the first harvest found that most participating households spent about the same amount on food as before.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
options: Likewise
However
For instance
Consequently
questions.explanation: The survey result contrasts with the association's expectation, so a contrast transition such as "However" is needed. "Consequently" would incorrectly present the unchanged spending as a result of the expectation.

questions.passage: For decades, historians described the 1913 flood in a small Ohio river town mainly through records left by city officials and railroad companies. More recently, a team led by Dr. Maya Chen at a local university has begun collecting letters, diary entries, and oral histories from families who lived on the town's east side. These sources show that residents relied on church networks and neighbors' boats long before official relief arrived. The project's director, Dr. Chen, argues that such documents do not merely add colorful details to the official account; they change our understanding of how the town survived.
questions.q: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: A new collection of personal accounts is revising historians' understanding of how a town's residents survived a flood.
Church networks were the only source of relief available after the flood.
City officials and railroad companies deliberately exaggerated the damage caused by the flood.
Diaries and oral histories are generally more accurate than official records.
questions.explanation: The passage emphasizes that newly collected letters, diaries, and oral histories change historians' understanding of survival, not merely add details. The claim that these sources are generally more accurate than official records goes beyond what the text states.

questions.passage: Mayor Daniel Cho's statement on the housing proposal was deliberately ______: its carefully balanced phrases could be read as either strong support for the plan or a warning about its costs, allowing supporters and opponents alike to quote it favorably.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
options: equivocal
caustic
succinct
categorical
questions.explanation: The statement's phrases can be read in two opposing ways, which makes the language ambiguous or "equivocal." "Categorical" means absolute and unambiguous, nearly the opposite of what the context describes.

questions.topic: Form, structure and sense (grammar and usage)
questions.passage: Hidden among the archived letters donated to the county historical society ______ a hand-drawn map that researchers believe shows the boundaries of the original farm.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: have been
were
was
are
questions.explanation: The subject is the singular phrase "a hand-drawn map," which appears after the verb in this inverted sentence, so the singular past-tense verb "was" is needed. "Were" and "are" are plural forms that do not agree with the subject.

questions.passage: The city's pilot program offered free rain barrels to homeowners in one neighborhood. Participation was highest among households that had already installed other water-saving devices. ______, program coordinator Elena Ruiz concluded that the free barrels mainly reinforced existing habits rather than attracting new participants.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
options: Similarly
Consequently
For instance
Nevertheless
questions.explanation: The organizers' conclusion follows logically from the finding that participation was highest among households already using water-saving devices. "Nevertheless" would signal a contrast, but the conclusion is presented as an inference from the preceding evidence.

questions.topic: Form, structure and sense (grammar and usage)
questions.passage: By the time the exhibit opens next month, the conservation team ______ more than two hundred photographs of the murals so that visitors can compare their current condition with their original appearance.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: will digitize
digitized
will have digitized
has digitized
questions.explanation: The action will be completed before a future event, which requires the future perfect "will have digitized." The simple past and present perfect do not express completion by a future time, and "will digitize" suggests the work begins then rather than being finished.

questions.passage: The historian's opening chapters are meticulously documented, but they are not ______: she seldom explains why a given petition or tax ledger matters, so readers without specialized knowledge may struggle to follow her argument.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
options: cursory
lucid
partisan
tentative
questions.explanation: The colon explains that the chapters are hard for general readers to follow because the author seldom clarifies the significance of documents, so they are not "lucid," or clear and easy to understand. "Cursory" means hasty or superficial, which conflicts with the claim that the chapters are meticulously documented.

questions.passage: Historian Maya Chen begins her study of a midwestern river town with census records showing modest population growth between 1880 and 1910. She then examines a local newspaper's advertisements, which grew sharply in number and variety. Only after establishing those patterns does Chen turn to residents' letters, using them to show how families understood their changing choices. The letters do not merely illustrate the trends; they help explain the desires behind them.
questions.q: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It summarizes a historical period and then questions the reliability of census records.
It traces a historian's sequence of sources and explains how the final source deepens the earlier findings.
It presents a historian's conclusion and then lists evidence that contradicts it.
It contrasts two towns to argue that advertisements are more trustworthy than letters.
questions.explanation: The text follows Chen's movement from census records to advertisements to letters, with the letters explaining the desires behind the trends. The other choices introduce comparisons, doubts about census accuracy, or contradictory evidence that the passage does not contain.

questions.passage:
A team of ecologists recorded native plant cover and the number of bee species observed in three neighborhood gardens. The table shows the results.
Garden | Native plant cover | Bee species observed
Maple | 12% | 5
Cedar | 35% | 11
Oak | 58% | 16
Which choice best describes the relationship shown in the table?
questions.q: Which choice best describes the relationship shown in the table?
options: As native plant cover increased across the three gardens, the number of bee species observed also increased.
Native plant cover was highest in Cedar, where 11 bee species were observed.
Cedar had more bee species than Oak did.
Maple had the greatest native plant cover but the fewest bee species observed.
questions.explanation: The table shows 12% cover with 5 bee species, 35% with 11, and 58% with 16, so both values rise together. The wrong choices misstate the garden with the highest cover or reverse the comparison between Cedar and Oak.

questions.passage:
Text 1: In a planning memo, museum educator Tomas Rivera argues that replacing printed labels with an audio guide makes exhibits more accessible. Visitors can listen at their own pace, he notes, and people with low vision can hear descriptions that printed text cannot provide.

Text 2: Curator Hana Ito agrees that audio guides can help some visitors, but she worries that they may discourage spontaneous conversation. In her view, a shared label often prompts strangers to talk about an object, while headphones can make a gallery feel more private.
questions.q: Which choice best describes the relationship between the two texts?
options: Text 2 proposes a solution that resolves the problem Text 1 identifies.
Text 2 argues that printed labels are inaccessible to all visitors, contradicting Text 1.
Text 2 accepts the accessibility benefit described in Text 1 but raises a different concern about audio guides.
Text 2 claims that audio guides cannot help visitors with low vision, which challenges Text 1's main claim.
questions.explanation: Text 2 grants that audio guides can help some visitors but adds a worry about reduced conversation. It does not deny the accessibility benefit, and it offers no solution that resolves Text 1's point.

questions.passage: In an essay on public art, critic Elena Ruiz describes a city's decision to install a sculpture in a busy plaza. She notes that officials expected the work to attract tourists and identify the area as a cultural destination. Ruiz then observes that local residents mainly used the sculpture as a meeting point, arranging to gather beneath it before walking to nearby shops. She concludes that public art's value cannot be measured only by tourism or official prestige, since everyday uses can be just as important.
questions.q: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: The essay shows that the sculpture failed to attract any visitors to the plaza.
The essay argues that a public artwork's everyday social uses can matter as much as its official purposes.
The essay explains why tourists are more important to public art than local residents are.
The essay claims that city officials should not install sculptures in busy plazas.
questions.explanation: Ruiz contrasts officials' expectations with residents' use of the sculpture as a meeting point and concludes that everyday uses matter. The passage does not reject public art, rank tourists above residents, or claim that no visitors came.

questions.passage:
A team of biologists surveyed three tide pools and recorded average water temperature and the number of sea anemones counted. The table shows the results.
Tide pool | Average water temperature (°C) | Sea anemones counted
North | 12 | 42
Center | 15 | 28
South | 18 | 13
Which choice best describes the data in the table?
questions.q: Which choice best describes the data in the table?
options: Sea anemones were most numerous where average water temperature was highest.
The North tide pool had the warmest water and the fewest sea anemones.
As average water temperature increased across the three tide pools, the number of sea anemones counted decreased.
The Center tide pool had more sea anemones than the North tide pool.
questions.explanation: The table shows that warmer tide pools had fewer anemones: 12°C with 42, 15°C with 28, and 18°C with 13. The other choices reverse the pattern or misread the counts.

questions.passage:
Text 1: In a school board report, analyst Priya Desai argues that moving high school start times later would improve attendance. Because adolescents' sleep patterns shift during the teen years, she writes, many students cannot fall asleep early enough to rest before an early bell.

Text 2: Teacher Marcus Lee agrees that later start times could help some students sleep more, but he notes that the change may create problems for students who work afternoon jobs or care for younger siblings. A later dismissal, he warns, could reduce the hours available for those responsibilities.
questions.q: Which choice best describes the relationship between the two texts?
options: Text 2 argues that later start times would improve attendance more than Text 1 claims.
Text 2 accepts a benefit described in Text 1 while identifying a practical drawback.
Text 2 disputes Text 1's claim that sleep patterns change during adolescence.
Text 2 proposes a schedule change that solves the problem Text 1 describes.
questions.explanation: Text 2 agrees that later start times could help students sleep but adds concerns about jobs and family care. It does not deny the sleep-pattern claim, promise greater attendance gains, or offer a solution.

questions.passage: In an article on urban coyotes, biologist Lena Ortiz begins by noting that residents often describe coyotes as fearless invaders. She then presents tracking data showing that most coyotes avoid busy roads and remain within green corridors. Ortiz concludes that the animals are not bold but simply follow habitat that people have inadvertently connected. The article's final sentence warns that labeling coyotes fearless may lead residents to overlook practical steps such as securing trash.
questions.q: Which choice best describes the function of the final sentence in the text?
options: It summarizes the residents' original description of coyotes as accurate.
It challenges the claim that coyotes avoid busy roads.
It introduces the tracking data that the article later explains.
It identifies a practical consequence of the misconception that the article has examined.
questions.explanation: The final sentence explains why calling coyotes fearless matters: residents may ignore steps like securing trash. It comes after the tracking evidence and questions, rather than confirms, the residents' description.

questions.passage:
A city compared recycling rates in three neighborhoods before and after adding curbside bins. The table shows the results.
Neighborhood | Before (%) | After (%)
East | 32 | 45
West | 28 | 39
North | 41 | 50
Which choice best describes the data in the table?
questions.q: Which choice best describes the data in the table?
options: The East neighborhood had a lower recycling rate before the bins were added than the West neighborhood did.
The North neighborhood had the largest increase in recycling rate of the three neighborhoods.
Recycling rates increased in all three neighborhoods after the bins were added, though by different amounts.
The West neighborhood had the highest recycling rate after the bins were added.
questions.explanation: Every neighborhood's rate rose: East increased by 13 points, West by 11, and North by 9. The North neighborhood did not have the largest increase, the West did not have the highest after-rate, and East's before-rate was higher than West's before-rate.

questions.passage: At the community theater's first dress rehearsal, Javier noticed that the painted backdrop for the bakery scene looked almost gray under the stage lights. During intermission, he borrowed a ladder and swapped two bulbs from the spare kit. In the second act, the loaf of bread on the backdrop seemed warm and golden, and several actors smiled as they crossed the stage. After the run, Javier wrote in his notebook: ______
questions.q: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: the actors proposed adding a bakery scene to the second act
the backdrop needed to be repainted before opening night
changing the stage lights had altered the backdrop's apparent color
the spare bulbs were too bright for the theater's electrical system
questions.explanation: Javier notices the backdrop appears gray, swaps bulbs, then sees it as warm and golden, so the notebook entry should reflect that lighting changed its perceived color. The repainting claim is unsupported, and the other choices introduce decisions or problems not shown. The electrical-system issue is also never suggested by the results.

questions.passage: Some city officials assume that planting trees will immediately reduce air temperature across an entire neighborhood. ______, the cooling effect is often strongest within a few dozen yards of each tree.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
options: Therefore
Similarly
In addition
However
questions.explanation: The second sentence qualifies the assumption by saying the cooling effect is limited in area, so a contrast transition is needed. The word that marks contrast is correct. The other transitions suggest cause, similarity, or addition, none of which fits the limiting relationship.

questions.passage:
• The Westside Community Center began a free after-school chess club in September.
• Attendance rose from 12 students in September to 31 in December.
• Students played against local retirees on Saturdays.
• A survey found that 84% of participants reported feeling more comfortable speaking in front of others.
questions.q: The student wants to write a sentence for a grant proposal that emphasizes the chess club's growth in participation and its reported benefit to students' confidence. Which choice best accomplishes the student's goal?
options: A survey of chess club participants found that 84% felt more comfortable speaking in front of others.
The Westside Community Center's chess club meets after school and on Saturdays with local retirees.
Since opening in September, the Westside Community Center's free chess club has grown from 12 to 31 students, and 84% of participants report feeling more comfortable speaking in front of others.
Attendance at the Westside Community Center's chess club rose from 12 to 31 students as local retirees volunteered.
questions.explanation: The sentence includes both the attendance increase from 12 to 31 and the survey result about greater comfort speaking in front of others. The other choices mention only one part or add unsupported details, such as retirees volunteering. Thus, it best serves the grant proposal's emphasis.

questions.passage: In the 1920s, the Larkspur Electric Company extended streetcar service to the working-class neighborhood of Elmwood. Over the next two years, weekly ridership from Elmwood rose from 600 to 2,100, and fare revenue from the neighborhood more than tripled. Yet the company's annual report called the extension only moderately profitable, noting that the new line required additional cars and extra evening service. These details suggest that ______
questions.q: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: the additional cars and evening service were unpopular with Elmwood riders
higher ridership and fare revenue did not necessarily translate into a large increase in the company's profits
the company had expanded service to Elmwood before studying demand
Elmwood residents soon demanded that the company lower its fares
questions.explanation: The passage shows ridership and revenue rising while the company still describes the line as only moderately profitable because it added costs. That supports the idea that more riders and fares did not guarantee much higher profit. The other choices introduce demands, planning failures, or rider dissatisfaction that the text never mentions.

questions.passage: The first reviews of Aisha Rahman's novel focused on its lively dialogue and fast-paced plot. ______, later critics have paid more attention to the novel's quiet descriptions of family meals and long walks, arguing that these scenes reveal the characters' changing relationships.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
options: By contrast
Therefore
Likewise
For instance
questions.explanation: The later critics focus on quiet descriptive scenes, which contrasts with the earlier reviewers' attention to lively dialogue and fast pacing. The phrase that signals contrast correctly marks that shift in emphasis. The other transitions suggest cause, similarity, or example rather than an opposing critical focus.

questions.passage:
• The Fairview Public Library launched a Book Bike in May.
• The Book Bike visits three parks each week.
• It lends children's books and signs people up for library cards.
• In its first summer, it issued 126 new library cards.
questions.q: The student wants to write a sentence for a library newsletter that emphasizes the Book Bike's reach and its success in signing up new patrons. Which choice best accomplishes the student's goal?
options: In its first summer, the Fairview Public Library's Book Bike visited three parks each week and helped 126 people sign up for library cards.
The Fairview Public Library issues library cards to children and adults.
The Book Bike lets children borrow books in parks.
The Book Bike visits three parks each week and lends children's books.
questions.explanation: The sentence includes the weekly visits to three parks, showing reach, and the 126 new library cards, showing success with new patrons. The other choices omit either the sign-up results or the extent of the program's reach. One choice also adds adults, which the notes do not mention.

questions.passage: Moths are often described as dull-colored, but some species have bright underwings. When a researcher placed models of a local moth on tree trunks, birds attacked the models with conspicuous wing patches more often than models with plain wings. However, when the same models were placed on dark forest floors, birds attacked the conspicuous and plain models at similar rates. These results suggest that ______
questions.q: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: tree trunks are the preferred resting place for all moths in the area
birds cannot see bright colors in forest habitats
the protective value of conspicuous wing patches depends on where a moth rests
plain-winged moths are always safer from birds than bright-winged moths are
questions.explanation: The conspicuous models were attacked more often on tree trunks but not on dark forest floors, so the background changes whether bright patches increase risk. The results do not show that birds are colorblind, that plain wings are always safer, or that all moths prefer tree trunks.

questions.passage: After the town opened a new pedestrian bridge over the river, nearby shops expected more foot traffic. ______, several stores reported that weekend sales changed little during the bridge's first month, since many walkers used the bridge for exercise and carried no wallets.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
options: However
Consequently
For example
Likewise
questions.explanation: The shops expected more foot traffic, but sales changed little, so a contrast transition is needed. The word that marks contrast correctly signals that unexpected result. The other transitions suggest a result, an illustration, or a similarity rather than a contrast.

questions.passage: In a three-year study of street trees in a mid-sized California city, a team of researchers compared 600 newly planted trees. Half stood along blocks where volunteers had agreed to water and monitor them; the other half received only routine municipal care. By the end of the study, 89 percent of the volunteer-monitored trees had survived, compared with 64 percent of the others. Tree species and planting-strip width were similar across both groups. The researchers concluded that the volunteers' regular attention, rather than the trees' physical setting, best explained the difference.
questions.q: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Street trees fail unless residents take over all maintenance from city crews.
Regular care from volunteers was linked to higher survival among newly planted street trees.
Municipal care is more effective than volunteer care for young street trees.
Tree species and planting-strip width determine whether street trees survive.
questions.explanation: The passage reports higher survival for volunteer-monitored trees and notes that species and planting-strip width were similar across groups, so the volunteers' attention best explains the difference. It does not claim that volunteers must replace all city care, nor that species or municipal crews were more important.

questions.passage: To study how people remember store layouts, a team of psychologists asked 120 volunteers to navigate a virtual grocery market. In one version, ingredients for a pasta sauce—tomatoes, garlic, mushrooms, and basil—were grouped on a single aisle with a clear sign. In another version, the same ingredients were scattered across four aisles without signs. Volunteers later located the ingredients more accurately in the grouped, signed version. The researchers cautioned that grouping alone may not help; in a follow-up, grouped aisles without labels produced no advantage over scattered products.
questions.q: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Grouping related products helped people remember locations only when the groups were also clearly labeled.
People remember grocery store layouts better when products are scattered across many aisles.
Virtual grocery markets are more difficult to navigate than real grocery stores.
Clear signs are unnecessary if products are grouped by the meals they help prepare.
questions.explanation: The text says that grouped, signed products were located more accurately, while grouped aisles without labels gave no advantage over scattered products. The benefit therefore depended on combining grouping with clear labeling, not on scattering products or making signs unnecessary.

questions.passage: A conservation group compared two methods for restoring native grasses on former farmland. At six sites, the group sowed seeds directly; at six similar sites, it first planted nursery-grown plugs. After two years, directly seeded plots had lower plant density but greater genetic diversity, while plug plots established ground cover faster and resisted erosion sooner. The group concluded that neither method was universally superior. Instead, the better choice depended on whether a site's most urgent need was rapid protection from erosion or long-term genetic resilience.
questions.q: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Two restoration methods offer different advantages, so the better method depends on a site's priorities.
Restoration projects should combine both methods to achieve every possible benefit equally.
Direct seeding is superior because it produces denser plant cover than nursery-grown plugs.
Nursery-grown plugs should be avoided because they reduce genetic diversity in restored grasslands.
questions.explanation: The text explains that direct seeding produced greater genetic diversity while nursery-grown plugs gave faster ground cover and erosion control, leading the group to say neither method was universally superior. The main point is that the better method depends on whether rapid erosion protection or long-term genetic resilience matters more; claims that one method is clearly best or that both must always be combined are unsupported.

questions.topic: Form, structure and sense (grammar and usage)
questions.passage: The stack of oral-history transcripts that social studies students collected over the past decade ______ now stored in the town archive, where residents can request copies by appointment.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: have been
is
are
were
questions.explanation: The subject is the singular noun 'stack', not the plural 'transcripts' in the intervening phrase, so the singular present verb 'is' is needed. 'Are' and 'were' agree with the plural noun but not with the subject, and 'have been' is likewise plural.

questions.topic: Form, structure and sense (grammar and usage)
questions.passage: The city's new heat plan adds shaded bus stops and public drinking fountains. ______, it will keep several air-conditioned libraries open as daytime shelters during heat waves.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
options: In addition
Nevertheless
As a result
For example
questions.explanation: The second sentence adds another feature of the heat plan, so the transition must signal addition. 'In addition' does that, while 'nevertheless' signals contrast, 'for example' signals illustration, and 'as a result' signals causation.

questions.topic: Form, structure and sense (grammar and usage)
questions.passage: Mateo is one of only a few volunteers in the program who ______ completed the advanced first-aid training required for overnight trail shifts.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: have
was
has
is
questions.explanation: The relative pronoun 'who' refers to the plural noun 'volunteers', so the plural auxiliary 'have' is needed before 'completed.' 'Has' would incorrectly agree with 'Mateo', while 'was' and 'is' do not form a logical present-perfect construction here.

questions.passage: The documentary's narration is unusually ______: it rarely states a conclusion outright, instead allowing viewers to draw inferences from interviews and archival footage.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
options: ornate
restrained
dogmatic
erratic
questions.explanation: 'Restrained' means held back or understated, which matches a narration that avoids stating conclusions outright and lets viewers infer them. 'Ornate' describes elaborate decoration, 'dogmatic' means forcefully asserting beliefs, and 'erratic' means unpredictable; none fits the controlled, indirect style described.

questions.passage: Although the committee's report acknowledged the need for more frequent bus service, it was notably ______ about how the city would pay for it, offering only vague references to future funding sources.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
options: meticulous
candid
forceful
noncommittal
questions.explanation: 'Noncommittal' means avoiding a clear position or promise, which matches the report's vague references to future funding sources. 'Candid' would suggest openness, 'meticulous' careful detail, and 'forceful' strong assertion—all contrary to the report's evasiveness.

questions.passage: City trees can lower street temperatures, but a tree planted in a narrow pit may struggle to survive. A recent program in a New England city paired each new street tree with a resident volunteer who watered it during dry weeks. The program's organizers initially worried that the volunteers would lose interest. After two summers, however, the survival rate for the paired trees was nearly twice that of trees cared for only by city crews.
questions.q: Which choice best describes the function of the last sentence in the text?
options: It describes the process by which volunteers were recruited.
It presents evidence that addresses a concern raised earlier in the text.
It introduces a new explanation for why narrow tree pits are harmful.
It compares the costs of volunteer care with those of city crews.
questions.explanation: The last sentence reports a survival-rate result that responds to the organizers' earlier worry about whether volunteers would stay committed. It does not explain why narrow tree pits are harmful, compare costs, or describe volunteer recruitment.

questions.passage: To understand why a neighborhood's public pool lost visitors, city planner Imani Brooks first interviewed residents. Many residents mentioned that the bus route no longer stopped near the pool. Brooks then compared attendance records with transit schedules and found that attendance fell most sharply after the route was shortened. Finally, Brooks proposed restoring a weekend stop. The report presents this sequence not as a simple story of cause and effect but as a case for testing a modest, reversible change.
questions.q: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It summarizes a debate between planners and residents about the pool's design.
It compares two neighborhoods that responded differently to a change in bus service.
It traces a problem from residents' observations to a comparison of records to a proposed solution.
It explains a scientific experiment by describing its hypothesis and control group.
questions.explanation: The text moves from residents' observations, to a comparison of attendance records with transit schedules, to a proposed weekend stop. It does not compare two neighborhoods, summarize a debate about pool design, or describe a controlled scientific experiment.

questions.passage:
A team of ecologists surveyed three urban parks to test whether greater native-plant cover is associated with more bird species. The team recorded native-plant cover and the number of bird species observed during standardized morning surveys. The results are shown in the table.

Park | Native-plant cover (%) | Bird species observed
Cedar Square | 18 | 11
Maple Green | 42 | 17
Riverbend Park | 63 | 22
questions.q: Which choice best describes the relationship shown in the table?
options: Native-plant cover caused the number of bird species to increase at each park.
Bird species observed remained about the same across the three parks.
Riverbend Park had the fewest bird species despite having the most native-plant cover.
Parks with greater native-plant cover tended to have more bird species observed.
questions.explanation: The table shows bird species increasing from 11 to 17 to 22 as native-plant cover rises from 18% to 42% to 63%. This is a positive association, but the survey does not establish that native-plant cover caused the increase, and the other descriptions contradict or ignore the pattern.

questions.passage:
A city transportation department measured the percentage of adults who reported walking at least 30 minutes on a typical day in three neighborhoods before and after new sidewalks were installed. The results are shown in the table.

Neighborhood | Before (%) | After (%)
Easton | 28 | 37
Lakeside | 41 | 46
Northfield | 33 | 34
questions.q: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the claim that the new sidewalks were followed by the largest increase in walking in Easton?
options: Northfield's after percentage was 34%, which was higher than Easton's before percentage of 28%.
All three neighborhoods showed an increase, which proves that new sidewalks cause residents to walk more.

The share of adults who reported walking at least 30 minutes on a typical day increased by 9 percentage points in Easton, compared with 5 percentage points in Lakeside and 1 percentage point in Northfield.
After the sidewalks were installed, Easton had 37% of adults walking at least 30 minutes, the highest percentage of any neighborhood.
questions.explanation: Easton rose from 28% to 37%, an increase of 9 percentage points; Lakeside rose from 41% to 46% (5 points), and Northfield rose from 33% to 34% (1 point). Thus the largest increase occurred in Easton. The statement that Easton had the highest after percentage is false because Lakeside's after percentage was 46%.

questions.passage:
Text 1: In an essay on city trees, landscape historian Maya Chen argues that street trees are most valuable for shading sidewalks and reducing heat at pedestrian level. She notes that large-canopy species can lower surface temperatures along a block and recommends planting them wherever sidewalks have room.

Text 2: Urban ecologist Daniel Ortiz agrees that street trees cool sidewalks, but he argues that this cooling benefit should not overshadow their role as habitat. In a study of a city's tree inventory, even small ornamental trees supported pollinators and birds, and he cautions that replacing diverse small trees with a few large shade species could reduce urban biodiversity.
questions.q: Based on the texts, how would Ortiz most likely respond to Chen's recommendation?
options: He would argue that planting large shade trees should not replace efforts to preserve diverse smaller trees, which provide habitat.
He would claim that ornamental trees are less valuable than large shade trees for supporting wildlife.
He would agree that cooling sidewalks is the only benefit of street trees worth considering.
He would recommend removing large shade trees from all city blocks.
questions.explanation: Ortiz agrees that street trees cool sidewalks, but he emphasizes that small ornamental trees also support pollinators and birds. His caution against replacing diverse small trees with a few large shade species directly qualifies Chen's recommendation.

questions.passage:
Text 1: Historian Elena Park argues that the 1950s expansion of suburban shopping centers in the town of Riverton weakened downtown businesses by drawing shoppers away. She cites declining sales at downtown stores after the centers opened.

Text 2: Another historian, Marcus Reed, agrees that shopping centers changed shopping patterns, but he notes that downtown Riverton businesses had already faced rising rents and aging buildings. He argues that the centers accelerated a decline that was underway rather than causing it.
questions.q: Which choice best describes the difference between the two texts?
options: Park presents shopping centers as a primary cause of downtown decline, while Reed sees them as speeding up a decline already underway.
Park argues that downtown businesses were unaffected by shopping centers, while Reed argues that they were destroyed.
Both historians claim that rising rents had no influence on downtown businesses.
Reed believes shopping centers improved downtown Riverton's sales, while Park believes they weakened them.
questions.explanation: Park emphasizes declining downtown sales after shopping centers opened and treats the centers as a main cause. Reed agrees that patterns changed but says rising rents and aging buildings had already begun the decline, so the centers accelerated it rather than caused it.

questions.passage: The museum extended its weekend hours in March______ attendance on Saturdays rose by nearly a third by May.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: ; therefore,
; however,
, therefore,
however,
questions.explanation: The blank joins two independent clauses that have a cause-and-effect relationship. A semicolon followed by the conjunctive adverb “therefore” correctly separates the clauses and signals that relationship; a comma before “therefore” creates a comma splice, and “however” signals contrast that the sentence does not have.

questions.passage: Although the bakery had been closed for nearly a decade______ the smell of cinnamon still seemed to linger in the empty storefront.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: no punctuation
questions.explanation: The word “Although” begins a subordinate clause that is followed by an independent clause, so a comma is needed at the boundary. A semicolon or colon cannot follow the subordinate clause, and leaving the boundary unpunctuated makes the sentence harder to parse and nonstandard.

questions.passage: For each seedling in the study, the botanist recorded three measurements______ stem height, leaf count, and root color.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: and
questions.explanation: A colon is appropriate after an independent clause to introduce the list of three measurements. A semicolon would require an independent clause after it, a comma cannot introduce this list in the same way, and “and” would misleadingly coordinate “three measurements” with the first item.

questions.passage: At the annual science fair, students from Ms. Okafor's class displayed projects on water filtration. The judges initially passed quickly by the table with the simplest model, a plastic bottle filled with sand, gravel, and charcoal. After the model filtered muddy water almost completely clear, however, several judges returned to ask the students how they had layered the materials. The judges' behavior most strongly suggests that ______
questions.q: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: they had underestimated the simple model before seeing how well it worked.
they were no longer interested in the other projects.
they believed the model contained no charcoal.
they thought the students had copied a published design.
questions.explanation: The judges first passed by the simple model, then returned to ask questions after it filtered muddy water almost completely clear. That change suggests they had not initially expected the model to work well; the text gives no support for claims about charcoal, copying, or losing interest in other projects.

questions.passage: A team of biologists studied two populations of mice in separate meadows. In one meadow, predators had been absent for decades; in the other, predators were common. The researchers placed mice from both populations in an unfamiliar enclosure with a simulated hawk call. Mice from the predator-free meadow froze less often and resumed foraging sooner than mice from the predator-heavy meadow. The researchers concluded that ______
questions.q: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: mice from the predator-heavy meadow were unable to hear the call.
mice from the predator-free meadow had not developed the same predator-response behavior as mice from the predator-heavy meadow.
predator presence had no lasting effect on mouse behavior.
the simulated hawk call was inaudible to all the mice.
questions.explanation: Mice from the predator-free meadow froze less and resumed foraging sooner when hearing a simulated hawk call, so their weaker response indicates they had not developed the same predator-response behavior. The data do not suggest hearing problems, inaudibility, or no effect of predator presence.

questions.passage: During the 1930s, a midwestern city's newly built public swimming pool was open to all residents on paper, but the city charged a small admission fee and required bathers to arrive with a new swimsuit. Attendance records show that the pool was used mostly by families from wealthier neighborhoods. In response, a neighborhood association began collecting used swimsuits and organizing free group walks to the pool. After the association's program began, attendance from poorer neighborhoods rose sharply. The passage most strongly suggests that ______
questions.q: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: the neighborhood association opposed public pools.
the admission fee and swimsuit requirement had discouraged some residents from using the pool.
wealthier families stopped using the pool after the program began.
the pool was officially segregated by race.
questions.explanation: Attendance from poorer neighborhoods rose sharply only after the association supplied swimsuits and organized free group walks, which addresses the fee and clothing barrier. The passage does not support claims about official racial segregation, opposition to pools, or wealthier families stopping their use.
